comment.comment: GNU m4 comments run from # to the next newline. Unlike most languages, m4 copies the comment (delimiters included) to its output verbatim instead of discarding it; it is still a comment in the sense that its contents are not macro-expanded. NOTE: if the file calls changecom(...) to pick different delimiters, this rule no longer matches the real comment syntax - see README for why that can't be tracked statically.
comment.name: comment.line.number-sign.m4

dnl-statement.comment: dnl is an ordinary builtin macro, but it works by blindly discarding raw characters up to and including the next newline (see skip_line() in input.c) - it does NOT respect quoting the way # comments do, so no nested patterns are applied inside it. Word boundaries include non-ASCII characters (the unicode-identifier dialect this extension targets - see README): in that dialect, x≡dnl is one identifier, not a dnl invocation.
dnl-statement.name: comment.line.dnl.m4

quoted-string.comment: Default-quoted m4 string: `...' with balanced nesting. changequote(...) can redefine the delimiters to anything at runtime; that is impossible to follow with a static grammar, so only the default backtick/apostrophe pair is recognized. See README. A quoted string is usually a deferred macro body, so its contents are tokenized as m4 code too (but comments/dnl are deliberately excluded here, since quoting inhibits both).
quoted-string.name: string.quoted.other.m4

quotable-code.comment: Shared building blocks that make sense both at the top level and inside a quoted string (which is usually just a not-yet-expanded macro body). Comments and dnl are intentionally NOT part of this set - both require unquoted, unexpanded top-level text.

directive-call.comment: Macros that change m4's own lexical rules at runtime. Highlighted distinctly as a reminder that everything after this call may no longer follow the syntax this grammar assumes.
directive-call.name: keyword.control.directive.m4

builtin-call.comment: GNU m4 builtin macro names. These are ordinary macros (users may redefine, undefine, or pushdef/popdef over them), so this is a lexical hint, not a guarantee that the name still means this at any given point in the file.
builtin-call.name: support.function.builtin.m4

macro-call.comment: Heuristic only: m4 has no syntax for 'this identifier is a macro' - ANY bare word can be a user-defined macro invocation, indistinguishable from literal text without evaluating define/pushdef elsewhere in the program (possibly in another included file). We highlight identifiers immediately followed by '(' (the m4 rule for 'this call takes arguments') as likely macro calls; bare words with no arguments are left unstyled since they are equally likely to be plain output text. See README. Identifiers may contain any non-ASCII character (equivalently, in UTF-8: any byte with the high bit set), supporting the unicode-identifier wrapper dialect described in the README; standard GNU m4 restricts words to ASCII [A-Za-z0-9_].
macro-call.name: entity.name.function.m4

parameter-reference.comment: $1.. $9, $0, $#, $*, $@ are only special while a macro body is being expanded; inside a quoted macro definition they are just literal characters until that point. Highlighted here as a readability aid for macro definitions.
parameter-reference.name: variable.parameter.m4

numeric-literal.comment: Covers the common decimal/0x/0b/0-octal forms accepted by eval(). GNU m4's eval() also accepts arbitrary radix literals of the form BASE:DIGITS (base 2-36); that form is not specially highlighted.
numeric-literal.name: constant.numeric.m4
